item.title: RoguePlanet Defender zero-day patched as AI coding agents face Friendly Fire and GhostApproval flaws
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft patches RoguePlanet Defender zero-day vulnerability — Must Read

Microsoft has patched the RoguePlanet zero-day in Microsoft Defender, tracked as CVE-2026-50656, via a Malware Protection Engine update. The flaw could let attackers gain SYSTEM privileges on fully patched Windows 10 and 11 systems using a race condition exploit.

  • Microsoft released a security patch for a Microsoft Defender zero-day vulnerability known as RoguePlanet, tracked as CVE-2026-50656.
  • The vulnerability was disclosed by a security researcher using the handle Nightmare Eclipse, who also shared a proof-of-concept exploit in a self-hosted Git repository.
  • Nightmare Eclipse said RoguePlanet affects fully patched Windows 10 and Windows 11 devices and can allow attackers to spawn a command prompt with SYSTEM privileges via a Microsoft Defender race condition.
  • Microsoft addressed the RoguePlanet vulnerability by releasing Microsoft Malware Protection Engine version 1.1.26060.3008.
  • Nightmare Eclipse has disclosed multiple other Windows zero-day exploits in recent months, including flaws affecting Microsoft Defender, BitLocker, and other Windows components.

Fake 7-Zip Installers Turn Devices Into Residential Proxy Nodes — Must Read

Researchers say a China-based actor dubbed Lurking Lizard has used fake 7-Zip installers, lookalike domains, and fake proxy-service brands to covertly turn victims’ devices into residential proxy nodes. The operation appears to be a full proxy-business ecosystem spanning victim recruitment, infrastructure, marketing, and monetization.

  • Infoblox researchers disclosed that a threat actor dubbed Lurking Lizard has operated a malicious residential proxy business using more than 230 lookalike domains since at least August 2022.
  • One campaign used a trojanized 7-Zip installer hosted on the lookalike domain 7zip[.]com to covertly recruit compromised devices as proxy nodes.
  • Lurking Lizard has impersonated major proxy providers including IPIDEA, SmartProxy, IP Royal, and 911Proxy, and has run fake independent review sites to direct traffic to its scam storefronts.
  • WHOIS analysis and infrastructure fingerprinting suggest that Lurking Lizard is a China-based actor, and the campaign has also used popular VPNs and services like HeroSMS as decoys to distribute proxy malware.
  • Infoblox said the operation spans victim acquisition, proxy infrastructure, marketing, and monetization, turning recruited devices into a pool that can be sold through lookalike proxy service brands.

GhostApproval Symlink Flaws Could Let Malicious Repos Run Code in AI Coding Agents — Should Read

Wiz researchers found that several AI coding assistants can be tricked by malicious repositories into writing through symlinks to sensitive files like SSH keys or shell startup scripts, while approval prompts show only harmless-looking paths. Some vendors have patched the issue, but users should update tools and avoid running agents on untrusted repos without sandboxing or limiting file access.

  • Wiz researchers identified a GhostApproval flaw in six AI coding assistants: Amazon Q Developer, Anthropic's Claude Code, Augment, Cursor, Google Antigravity, and Windsurf.
  • The attack uses a malicious repository with a symbolic link, such as a project_settings.json file that actually points to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, causing an assistant-approved write to modify a sensitive file instead.
  • Wiz found that approval dialogs can show the harmless-looking symlink path rather than the real file being modified, creating what it calls an informed-consent bypass.
  • As of publication, Amazon Q Developer, Cursor, and Google Antigravity had shipped fixes, Augment and Windsurf had acknowledged the issue without fixes, and Anthropic disputed that Claude Code behavior was a bug.
  • Wiz recommended that tool makers resolve symlinks and show the true destination before asking for approval, flag writes outside the project folder, and avoid touching disk before the user approves.

Top AI Agents Built to Catch Malicious Code Can Be Tricked Into Running It — Should Read

AI Now researchers showed that autonomous AI coding agents like Claude Code and OpenAI Codex can be tricked by instructions in a repository README into running malicious scripts while reviewing untrusted code. The key takeaway is that agents with command execution should not be used on untrusted projects without strict human approval and isolation, because model safety checks are not reliable containment.

  • AI Now Institute researchers published a proof-of-concept called Friendly Fire showing that Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex can be tricked into running attacker-controlled code when autonomous command-approval modes are enabled.
  • The tested setups included Claude Code CLI versions 2.1.116, 2.1.196, 2.1.198, and 2.1.199 on Claude Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 5, or Opus 4.8, and OpenAI Codex CLI 0.142.4 on GPT-5.5.
  • The demo placed extra files in the geopy Python library, used a README note to suggest running security.sh, and had that script quietly launch a hidden binary carrying the real payload.
  • The researchers said there is no patch to wait for because the weakness is in the workflow design, where agents cannot reliably separate untrusted repository text from instructions they should follow.
  • The article states there is no reported exploitation in the wild, the public GitHub code has the payload stripped, and the proof-of-concept stops at initial code execution without privilege escalation or lateral movement.
